claim: CBS expression and transsulfuration pathway activity are elevated in AKT-induced senescence (AIS).
source: An increase of CBS protein expression was observed in BJ3 human skin fibroblasts expressing telomerase reverse transcriptase (BJ-TERT) (Figure 1B) and IMR90 human fetal lung fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) overexpressing myristoylated (myr)-AKT1.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased CBS protein in cells overexpressing myrAKT1 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: AKT hyperactivation does not affect CBS mRNA expression.
source: However, AKT hyperactivation did not affect CBS mRNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism underpinning increased CBS protein expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing no significant change in CBS mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: CTH and xCT are upregulated in AIS cells compared to proliferating control cells.
source: Both CTH and xCT were upregulated in AIS cells compared to proliferating control cells, suggesting an elevated cysteine synthesis via the transsulfuration pathway and cysteine uptake (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased CTH and xCT protein levels in AIS cells (Figure 1B).

claim: A significant increase in transsulfuration pathway activity was observed in BJ-TERT fibroblasts upon AKT but not HRAS hyperactivation.
source: A significant increase in transsulfuration pathway activity was observed in BJ-TERT fibroblasts upon AKT but not HRAS hyperactivation (Figure 1C), suggesting that activation of transsulfuration pathway is a specific cellular response to constitutive activation of AKT.
evidence: Supported by H2S production measurements showing increased activity in myrAKT1 but not HRASG12V cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Inhibition of H2S production by aminoxyacetate (AOAA) impairs cell proliferation of BJ-TERT cells overexpressing myrAKT1.
source: Inhibition of H2S production by aminoxyacetate (AOAA) (Szabo, 2016) impaired cell proliferation (Figure 1D) and increased SA-βGal activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) of BJ-TERT cells overexpressing myrAKT1.
evidence: Supported by cell confluency measurements and SA-βGal staining data (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Cysteine deprivation does not affect the survival of AIS cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, cysteine deprivation potently increased the expression of CBS and CTH in AIS cells (Figure 1B) and did not affect the survival of AIS cells (Figure 1E), indicating that increased cysteine level in AIS cells due to elevated transsulfuration pathway activity is critical for cell viability.
evidence: Supported by cell confluency measurements showing no decrease in AIS cell survival under cysteine-free conditions (Figure 1E).

claim: Loss of CBS in AIS cells significantly decreases the proportion of cells with SA-βGal activity.
source: Loss of CBS in AIS cells significantly decreased the proportion of cells with SA-βGal activity, increased EdU incorporation, and enhanced colony formation, demonstrating an essential role of CBS in AIS maintenance (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by SA-βGal staining, EdU incorporation, and colony formation assay data (Figure 2B).

claim: CBS depletion induced by doxycycline decreases SA-βGal activity and increases EdU incorporation in AIS cells.
source: Upon expressing myrAKT1, these cells underwent AIS, as indicated by a significant increase in SA-βGal-positive cells and decrease in EdU-positive cells and, consistent with the finding in the AIS escape siRNA screen, CBS depletion induced by doxycycline decreased SA-βGal activity, and increased EdU incorporation in AIS cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by SA-βGal staining and EdU incorporation data in doxycycline-inducible CBS knockdown cells (Figure 2D).

claim: Simultaneously expressing ER-CBS prevents senescence escape of CBS-depleted cells.
source: Importantly, simultaneously expressing ER-CBS prevented senescence escape of CBS-depleted cells, confirming the on-target specificity of the knockdown and the critical role of CBS in maintaining AIS (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by SA-βGal and EdU data showing rescue of senescence phenotype upon CBS re-expression (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Modulation of CBS expression in proliferating control cells does not affect the percentage of SA-βGal- and EdU-positive cells.
source: Modulation of CBS expression in proliferating control cells did not affect the percentage of SA-βGal- and EdU-positive cells (Figure 2D), suggesting that the effect of CBS depletion on cell proliferation is specific for AIS cells.
evidence: Supported by SA-βGal and EdU data in pBabe control cells (Figure 2D).

claim: Knockdown of CBS in BJ-TERT cells with constitutive RAS activation does not affect colony formation.
source: Knockdown of CBS in BJ-TERT cells with constitutive RAS activation did not affect colony formation, suggesting CBS has a specific regulatory role for AIS but not RIS maintenance (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in HRASG12V-expressing cells (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Loss of CBS does not affect the mRNA and protein expression level of several key SASP-related genes including IL1A, IL1B, IL6, and IL8 in AIS cells.
source: While loss of CBS released AIS cells from cell cycle arrest, knockdown of CBS did not significantly change the mRNA and protein expression level of several key SASP-related genes including IL1A, IL1B, IL6, and IL8, which are upregulated during AIS (Astle et al., 2012; Chan et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data showing no significant change in SASP factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).

claim: p53 and its downstream target p21 are upregulated during AIS, but depletion of CBS has no effect on these levels.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, p53 and its downstream target p21 were upregulated during AIS, but depletion of CBS had no effect on these levels.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing p53 and p21 levels remain unchanged upon CBS depletion (Figure 2F).

claim: Total Rb and its inhibitory phosphorylated form at serine 807/811 are markedly suppressed in AIS and partially rescued upon CBS knockdown.
source: Furthermore, total Rb, a key regulator of the G1/S phase transition, and its inhibitory phosphorylated form at serine 807/811 were markedly suppressed in AIS and partially rescued upon CBS knockdown.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing changes in Rb and phospho-Rb levels (Figure 2F).

claim: Cyclin A is upregulated upon depleting CBS in AIS cells.
source: Cyclin A, which mediates S to G2/M phase cell cycle progression, was also upregulated upon depleting CBS in AIS cells.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased Cyclin A levels (Figure 2F).

claim: CBS depletion demonstrates that CBS loss can restore the proliferation of cells that have undergone AIS in a p53-independent manner.
source: These results demonstrate that CBS depletion can restore the proliferation of cells that have undergone AIS in a p53-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CBS depletion restores proliferation without affecting p53 levels.

claim: siRNA knockdown of genes involved in the transsulfuration and transmethylation pathway (except CBS) does not significantly affect AIS cell numbers.
source: By analysis of the data from the AIS escape siRNA screen, we found that except CBS, siRNA knockdown of other genes involved in the transsulfuration and transmethylation pathway did not significantly affect AIS cell numbers (robust Z score <2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by siRNA screen data showing robust Z scores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Knockdown of CBS does not affect the expression levels of CTH and xCT when BJ-TERT cells are grown in cysteine-replete culture medium.
source: In addition, knockdown of CBS did not affect the expression levels of CTH and xCT when BJ-TERT cells were grown in cysteine-replete culture medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no change in CTH and xCT levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: AIS cells show increased abundance of serine, glycine, and glutamate, the metabolites involved in transsulfuration pathway and GSH synthesis.
source: AIS cells showed increased abundance of serine, glycine, and glutamate, the metabolites involved in transsulfuration pathway and GSH synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by GC/MS metabolomics data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Loss of CBS does not affect abundance of serine, glycine, and glutamate but results in an increased level of homocysteine.
source: Loss of CBS did not affect abundance of these metabolites but resulted in an increased level of Hcy, suggesting loss of CBS causes an accumulation of the upstream substrate Hcy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by GC/MS metabolomics data showing increased homocysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: AIS cells display a small but significant fraction of 13C labeled cysteine and GSH along with a significant increase of total levels of serine, cysteine, and GSH.
source: However, AIS cells displayed a small but significant fraction of 13C labeled cysteine and GSH along with a significant increase of total levels of serine, cysteine, and GSH (Figure 3B-E), indicating upregulation of transsulfuration pathway activity during AIS.
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing LC/MS data (Figure 3B-E).

claim: A significant decrease of cystathionine abundance was observed in CBS-depleted AIS cells.
source: Consistent with the role of CBS in catalyzing de novo cystathionine synthesis, a significant decrease of cystathionine abundance was observed in CBS-depleted AIS cells.
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data showing decreased cystathionine levels (Figure 3C).

claim: The abundance of cysteine and GSH is not affected by CBS depletion in cysteine-replete conditions.
source: Notably, the abundance of cysteine and GSH was not affected by CBS depletion (Figure 3D and E) and neither was H2S production (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data showing no change in cysteine and GSH levels (Figure 3D and E) and H2S production measurements (Figure 3F).

claim: Deprivation of cysteine from the medium markedly diminishes the intracellular cysteine and GSH abundance in AIS cells.
source: Indeed, deprivation of cysteine from the medium markedly diminished the intracellular cysteine and GSH abundance in AIS cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data showing decreased cysteine and GSH levels under cysteine-free conditions (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Increase of cystathionine was observed in cysteine-depleted conditions, possibly attributed to a marked upregulation of CBS expression.
source: On the other hand, increase of cystathionine was observed in the cysteine-depleted conditions (Figure 3C), possibly attributed to a marked upregulation of CBS expression observed in AIS cells after cysteine deprivation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data showing increased cystathionine (Figure 3C) and Western blot data showing increased CBS expression (Figure 1B).

claim: The viability of both proliferating cells and AIS cells is decreased after treatment with erastin and further suppressed by CBS knockdown.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the viability of both proliferating cells and AIS cells was decreased after treatment with erastin, an inhibitor of cystine-glutamate antiporter Xc-, and further suppressed by CBS knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability measurements after erastin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Pathways involved in oxidative phosphorylation and ROS are significantly downregulated in CBS-depleted AIS cells compared to control AIS cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the hallmark gene sets in the molecular signatures database (MSigDB) identified that pathways involved in oxidative phosphorylation and ROS were significantly downregulated in CBS-depleted AIS cells compared to the control AIS cells (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data (Figure 3G and H).

claim: CBS localizes to both the cytoplasm and mitochondria.
source: CBS has been reported to localize to both the cytoplasm and mitochondria and regulate mitochondrial function and ATP synthesis via H2S (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Panagaki et al., 2019). Consistent with this, we also observed CBS localization in the mitochondria by immunofluorescent cell staining (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining data (Figure 4A and B) and citations to previous studies (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Panagaki et al., 2019).

claim: AIS cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial abundance compared to proliferating cells.
source: AIS cells exhibited elevated mitochondrial abundance as indicated by increased intensity of MitoTracker-Deep Red staining compared to proliferating cells (Figure 4A), consistent with an increased abundance of proteins involved in the mitochondrial electron transport chain as detected by Western blotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker staining data (Figure 4A) and Western blot data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: AIS cells display increased mitochondrial CBS abundance.
source: The mitochondrial localization of CBS was further supported by Western blotting of mitochondrial extracts isolated from AIS and proliferating cells (Figure 4C). AIS cells displayed increased mitochondrial CBS abundance.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data of mitochondrial fractions (Figure 4C).

claim: C-terminally FLAG-tagged CBS is present in intact mitochondria and is resistant to protease treatment.
source: The C-terminally FLAG-tagged CBS was present in intact mitochondria and was resistant to protease treatment and only degraded upon membrane solubilization by Triton X-100.
evidence: Supported by protease protection assay data (Figure 4D).

claim: Loss of CBSD2 motif abrogates CBS mitochondrial localization.
source: Consistent with a previous finding (Teng et al., 2013), loss of CBSD2 motif abrogated CBS mitochondrial localization (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data of mitochondrial fractions (Figure 4F) and citation to previous study (Teng et al., 2013).

claim: Expression of wild type CBS prevents AIS escape while cells expressing the truncation mutant still escape from AIS.
source: Expression of wild type CBS prevented AIS escape as evidenced by a decrease of EdU-positive cells and increase of SA-βGal-positive cells while cells expressing the truncation mutant still escaped from AIS (Figure 4G and H), demonstrating that mitochondrial localization of CBS is required to maintain AIS.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation and SA-βGal staining data (Figure 4G and H).

claim: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP production are markedly elevated during AIS.
source: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP production were markedly elevated during AIS and knockdown of CBS significantly suppressed basal OCR and ATP production (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data (Figure 5B and C).

claim: Knockdown of CBS significantly suppresses basal OCR and ATP production in AIS cells.
source: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and ATP production were markedly elevated during AIS and knockdown of CBS significantly suppressed basal OCR and ATP production (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data (Figure 5B and C).

claim: Knockdown of CBS in RIS cells has an opposite effect on oxidative phosphorylation by further upregulating basal OCR and ATP production.
source: While basal OCR was also increased during RIS, knockdown of CBS in RIS cells, in contrast to those undergoing AIS, had an opposite effect on oxidative phosphorylation by further upregulating basal OCR and ATP production (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data (Figure 5B and C).

claim: Reconstitution with wild type CBS rescues basal OCR and ATP production levels in CBS-depleted AIS cells.
source: Reconstitution with wild type CBS rescued basal OCR and ATP production levels in CBS-depleted AIS cells. In contrast, AIS cells expressing C-terminal truncated CBS protein failed to restore basal OCR and ATP production (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data (Figure 5E and F).

claim: AIS cells expressing C-terminal truncated CBS protein fail to restore basal OCR and ATP production.
source: Reconstitution with wild type CBS rescued basal OCR and ATP production levels in CBS-depleted AIS cells. In contrast, AIS cells expressing C-terminal truncated CBS protein failed to restore basal OCR and ATP production (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data (Figure 5E and F).

claim: Treatment of AIS cells with antioxidant Trolox results in increased proliferation and decreased SA-βGal staining.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first treated AIS cells with an antioxidant Trolox, which resulted in increased proliferation (Figure 4G) and decreased SA-βGal staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), establishing the role of oxidative stress in AIS maintenance.
evidence: Supported by cell confluency measurements (Figure 4G) and SA-βGal staining data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: CBS knockdown decreases ROS levels in AIS cells.
source: Critically, CBS knockdown decreased ROS levels in AIS cells (Figure 5H and I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis of ROS production (Figure 5H and I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: CBS genetic alterations are found in gastric cancer.
source: Analysis of TCGA stomach adenocarcinoma data from 478 samples using cBioPortal (http://www.cbioportal.org) identified CBS deep deletions and mutations in gastric cancer (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis (Figure 6A).

claim: PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling pathway alterations occur in 33% of gastric cancer.
source: Further analysis of the TCGA gastric cancer patient data revealed that PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling pathway alterations occur in 33% of gastric cancer (142 of 441 samples) with PIK3CA, AKT, and PTEN alterations being the most common genetic alterations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CBS genetic alterations were found in 18 of 441 gastric cancers with 12 cases cooccurring with mutations in PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway.
source: CBS genetic alterations were found in 18 of 441 gastric cancers with 12 cases cooccurring with mutations in PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis.

claim: There is a significant association between CBS mutations and PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway activation.
source: There was a significant association between CBS mutations and PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway activation (p-value = 0.0031, 95% CI = 1.5202–14.9139 and odds ratio 4.4905).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of TCGA data.

claim: CBS mRNA level is significantly decreased in tumors compared to adjacent normal tissues in gastric cancer patients.
source: Furthermore, CBS mRNA level was significantly decreased in tumors (N=406) compared to adjacent normal tissues (N=211) in gastric cancer patients (Figure 6B), consistent with the hypothesis that CBS is a tumor suppressor in gastric cancers characterized by PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway alterations.
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis (Figure 6B).

claim: Cytosolic CBS protein expression level is significantly downregulated in tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal gastric tissues.
source: Cytosolic CBS protein expression level, as measured by the percentage of cells with positive CBS staining (Figure 5D), and fluorescence intensity (Figure 6E) were significantly downregulated in tumor tissues compared to the adjacent normal gastric tissues.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining data from tissue microarray (Figure 6D and E).

claim: CBS expression is markedly decreased in all gastric cancer cell lines tested compared to gastric epithelial cells.
source: Compared to gastric epithelial cells, CBS expression was markedly decreased in all gastric cancer cell lines while elevated AKT activity, as indicated by increase of AKT phosphorylation, was observed in AGS, Hs746T, KATO III gastric cancer cell lines (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data (Figure 6F).

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between CBS mRNA expression level and DNA methylation in gastric cancer cell lines.
source: Comparison of CBS mRNA expression with DNA methylation status in a panel of 34 human gastric cancer cell lines revealed a significant negative correlation between CBS mRNA expression level and DNA methylation (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data (Figure 6G).

claim: The CBS promoter is methylated in all six gastric cancer cell lines tested.
source: Indeed, the CBS promoter was methylated in all six gastric cancer cell lines tested, and half of them displayed complete absence of unmethylated CBS promoter (SNU-1, NCI-N87, and AGS) that was associated with undetectable CBS transcription (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by methylation-specific PCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Blocking DNA methylation with azacitidine upregulates CBS mRNA expression in gastric cancer cell lines.
source: Blocking DNA methylation with azacitidine, a DNA methyltransferase-inhibiting cytosine nucleoside analogue upregulated CBS mRNA expression in all cell lines tested except Hs746T, whereby SNU-1 cells showed a>50-fold increase, confirming epigenetic silencing of CBS expression in gastric cancer cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data after azacitidine treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).

claim: AKT hyperactivation increases transsulfuration pathway activity and GSH production in GES-1 cells, which is not affected by CBS depletion.
source: Consistent with our results in fibroblasts, AKT hyperactivation increased transsulfuration pathway activity and GSH production, which was not affected by CBS depletion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by H2S production and GSH measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: Hyperactivation of AKT1 effectively promotes anchorage-independent growth of GES-1 cells, which is further enhanced by CBS depletion.
source: However, it effectively promoted anchorage-independent growth, and this was further enhanced by CBS depletion (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data (Figure 7B).

claim: CBS depletion significantly enhances anchorage-independent growth of GES-1 cells with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated PTEN knockout.
source: CBS depletion also significantly enhanced anchorage-independent growth of GES-1 cells with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9-mediated PTEN knockout (Figure 7C–D) but not in 2D cell culture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data (Figure 7C–D) and 2D cell culture data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Restoration of wild type CBS increases H2S production in AGS cells.
source: Restoration of wild type CBS increased H2S production (Figure 7F) but did not significantly enhance GSH abundance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by H2S production measurements (Figure 7F) and GSH measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Restoration of CBS expression does not significantly enhance GSH abundance in AGS cells.
source: Restoration of wild type CBS increased H2S production (Figure 7F) but did not significantly enhance GSH abundance (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by GSH measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Restoration of CBS expression does not affect AGS cell proliferation in 2D cell culture.
source: Interestingly, restoration of CBS expression did not affect AGS cell proliferation in 2D cell culture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell confluency measurements (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Induction of wild type CBS significantly suppresses AGS tumor growth in vivo.
source: Induction of CBSwt significantly suppressed AGS tumor growth (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements in xenograft model (Figure 7G).

claim: Induction of CBS is associated with a marked decrease in Ki67 expression and inhibitory RB phosphorylation without altering p53 and p21 expression levels in tumor tissues.
source: Induction of CBS was also associated with a marked decrease in Ki67 expression and inhibitory RB phosphorylation without altering p53 and p21 expression levels in the tumor tissues, suggesting that restoration of CBS expression could suppress gastric tumor formation independent of p53 (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and IHC data from tumor tissues (Figure 7H, I).

claim: Activation of AKT can increase intracellular ROS levels by stimulating oxidative phosphorylation and impairing ROS scavenging by inhibition of FoxO transcription factors.
source: Activation of AKT can also increase intracellular ROS levels by stimulating oxidative phosphorylation and impairing ROS scavenging by inhibition of FoxO transcription factors (Nogueira et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Nogueira et al., 2008).

claim: Increased mitochondrial abundance and respiratory activity, as well as ROS production, are observed in senescent-like cells resulting from AKT hyperactivation.
source: Consistent with these findings, we demonstrate increased mitochondrial abundance and respiratory activity, as well as ROS production in the senescent-like cells resulting from AKT hyperactivation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased mitochondrial markers, OCR, and ROS levels.

claim: Alleviation of oxidative stress by antioxidant treatment partially releases AIS cells from cell division arrest.
source: Alleviation of oxidative stress by antioxidant treatment partially releases AIS cells from cell division arrest, supporting that ROS is required for AIS maintenance.
evidence: Supported by Trolox treatment data showing increased proliferation and decreased SA-βGal staining.

claim: AKT activation markedly increases xCT protein expression, indicating increased extracellular cystine uptake in AIS.
source: We found that AKT activation markedly increased xCT protein expression, a cystine-glutamate antiporter encoded by SLC7A11, indicating the increase of extracellular cystine uptake in AIS.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased xCT levels.

claim: In cysteine-replete conditions, AIS cells exhibit elevated intracellular cysteine level and subsequent increased production of GSH and H2S.
source: Isotope tracing coupled with LC-MS analysis revealed that in cysteine-replete conditions AIS cells exhibited an elevated intracellular cysteine level and subsequent increased production of GSH and H2S, the critical components in the antioxidant system, which was abrogated by cysteine deprivation.
evidence: Supported by isotope tracing LC-MS data.

claim: H2S inhibits H2O2-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction by preserving the protein expression levels and activity of key antioxidant enzymes, inhibiting ROS production and lipid peroxidation.
source: Previous studies have shown that H2S inhibits H2O2-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction by preserving the protein expression levels and activity of key antioxidant enzymes, inhibiting ROS production and lipid peroxidation (Wen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Wen et al., 2013).

claim: At low concentrations, H2S acts as a mitochondrial electron donor to mitochondrial complex II, resulting in bioenergetic stimulation.
source: At low concentrations, H2S acts as a mitochondrial electron donor to mitochondrial complex II, resulting in bioenergetic stimulation (Szabo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Szabo et al., 2013).

claim: At high concentrations, H2S acts as a mitochondrial poison via the inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondrial complex IV.
source: At high concentrations, H2S acts as a mitochondrial poison via the inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondrial complex IV (Panagaki et al., 2019; Szabo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Panagaki et al., 2019; Szabo et al., 2014).

claim: Suppression of H2S by AOAA exacerbates proliferative arrest of AKT-hyperactivated cells, supporting a protective effect of H2S from oxidative stress-induced cell death.
source: Our finding that suppression of H2S by AOAA exacerbates proliferative arrest of AKT-hyperactivated cells supports a protective effect of H2S from oxidative stress-induced cell death (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by cell confluency data after AOAA treatment (Figure 1D).

claim: myrAKT1-expressing cells are resistant to exogenous cysteine deprivation.
source: The protective role of the transsulfuration pathway in AIS is further supported by the finding that myrAKT1-expressing cells are resistant to exogenous cysteine deprivation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by cell confluency data under cysteine-free conditions (Figure 1E).

claim: In AIS cells, CBS mitochondrial localization is enhanced, resulting in an increase of ROS production through upregulated mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, we found that under cysteine-replete conditions, CBS depletion did not affect the production of antioxidants (GSH and H2S) downstream of the transsulfuration pathway. Instead, in AIS cells CBS mitochondrial localization was enhanced, resulting in an increase of ROS production through upregulated mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, which contributes to maintenance of AIS status (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial fractionation, OCR, and ROS measurements.

claim: Overproduction of H2S by increased mitochondrial-localized CBS expression results in suppression of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production in fibroblasts from Down syndrome patients.
source: Intriguingly, a recent publication reported that overproduction of H2S by increased mitochondrial-localized CBS expression results in suppression of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production in the fibroblasts from Down syndrome patients (Panagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Panagaki et al., 2019).

claim: A negative correlation between CBS and xCT expression is observed in gastric cancer cell lines.
source: In parallel, a negative correlation between CBS and xCT expression was observed in gastric cancer cell lines, which is consistent with a recent report that cancer cells maintain intracellular cysteine levels and sustain cell proliferation by increasing xCT-mediated cysteine uptake (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data and citation to previous study (Zhu et al., 2019).

claim: Induction of apoptosis and impairment of gastric cancer cell metastasis by increasing H2S production upon NaHS treatment has been previously reported.
source: Induction of apoptosis and impairment of gastric cancer cell metastasis by increasing H2S production upon NaHS treatment has been previously reported (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: CBS is a novel regulator of AIS maintenance.
source: Taken together, our study identifies CBS as a novel regulator of AIS maintenance and a potential tumor suppressor in gastric cancer pathogenesis, potentially providing a new metabolic vulnerability that can be harnessed to target PI3K/AKT/mTORC1-driven cancers.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings showing CBS is required for AIS maintenance.

claim: CBS is a potential tumor suppressor in gastric cancer pathogenesis.
source: Taken together, our study identifies CBS as a novel regulator of AIS maintenance and a potential tumor suppressor in gastric cancer pathogenesis, potentially providing a new metabolic vulnerability that can be harnessed to target PI3K/AKT/mTORC1-driven cancers.
evidence: Supported by data showing CBS loss cooperates with PI3K/AKT activation in gastric cancer and CBS restoration suppresses tumor growth.

claim: Hyperactivation of oncogenic pathways downstream of RAS and PI3K/AKT in normal cells induces a senescence-like phenotype that acts as a tumor-suppressive mechanism.
source: Hyperactivation of oncogenic pathways downstream of RAS and PI3K/AKT in normal cells induces a senescence-like phenotype that acts as a tumor-suppressive mechanism that must be overcome during transformation.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: AIS is characterized by common senescence hallmarks including cell cycle arrest, SASP, global transcriptional changes, and metabolic hyperactivity.
source: AIS is characterized by the common senescence hallmarks including cell cycle arrest, a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), global transcriptional changes, and metabolic hyperactivity (Chan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Chan et al., 2020).

claim: AIS does not display p16 upregulation, a DNA damage response, or senescence-associated heterochromatin foci.
source: Distinct from RIS, AIS does not display either p16 upregulation, a DNA damage response or senescence-associated heterochromatin foci.
evidence: Supported by established findings from previous studies.

claim: AIS is associated with elevated p53 expression through increased mTORC1-dependent translation and reduced HDM2 dependent destabilization.
source: Instead, AIS is associated with elevated p53 expression through increased mTORC1-dependent translation and reduced human double minute 2 (HDM2) dependent destabilization (Astle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Astle et al., 2012).

claim: CBS converts homocysteine to cystathionine which is subsequently hydrolyzed by CTH to form cysteine, the crucial precursor for GSH production.
source: CBS converts homocysteine (Hcy), a key metabolite in the transmethylation pathway, to cystathionine which is subsequently hydrolyzed by cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH) to form cysteine, the crucial precursor for GSH production (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by established biochemical knowledge and schematic diagram (Figure 1).

claim: CBS catalyzes the production of H2S, a diffusible gaseous transmitter that modulates mitochondrial function and cellular bioenergetics.
source: CBS also catalyzes the production of H2S, a diffusible gaseous transmitter that modulates mitochondrial function and cellular bioenergetics (Szabo et al., 2013; Szabo et al., 2014; Módis et al., 2014), exerts antioxidant effects through inhibition of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and lipid peroxidation (Wen et al., 2013), and stimulates antioxidant production via sulfhydration of key proteins involved in antioxidant defense such as Keap1 and p66Shc (Paul and Snyder, 2012; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Szabo et al., 2013; Szabo et al., 2014; Módis et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2013; Paul and Snyder, 2012; Yang et al., 2013).

claim: CBS acts through control of Hcy, H2S, and GSH metabolism and exerts diverse biological functions including regulating DNA methylation, mitochondrial respiration, and redox homeostasis.
source: Thus, CBS acts through control of Hcy, H2S, and GSH metabolism and exerts diverse biological functions including regulating DNA methylation, mitochondrial respiration, and redox homeostasis (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: CBS plays a complex role in cancer pathogenesis having purported tumor-promoting and -suppressive roles.
source: CBS plays a complex role in cancer pathogenesis having purported tumor-promoting and -suppressive roles.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing context-dependent roles of CBS in different cancers.

claim: Activation of CBS promoted tumor growth in colon, ovarian, breast, prostate, and lung cancers.
source: Activation of CBS promoted tumor growth in colon (Phillips et al., 2017; Szabo et al., 2013), ovarian (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), breast (Sen et al., 2015), prostate (Liu et al., 2016), and lung cancers (Szczesny et al., 2016), whereas loss of CBS in glioma cells increased tumor volume in vivo (Takano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Phillips et al., 2017; Szabo et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Sen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016; Szczesny et al., 2016; Takano et al., 2014).

claim: Loss of CBS in glioma cells increased tumor volume in vivo.
source: Activation of CBS promoted tumor growth in colon (Phillips et al., 2017; Szabo et al., 2013), ovarian (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), breast (Sen et al., 2015), prostate (Liu et al., 2016), and lung cancers (Szczesny et al., 2016), whereas loss of CBS in glioma cells increased tumor volume in vivo (Takano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Takano et al., 2014).

claim: The function of CBS in liver cancer remains inconclusive with conflicting reports of both tumor-promoting and -suppressive roles.
source: In addition, the function of CBS in liver cancer remains inconclusive with conflicting reports of both tumor-promoting (Jia et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2012) and -suppressive roles (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jia et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2009).

claim: Oxidative stress is a key metabolic feature of RAS-induced senescence and ROS triggers DNA damage and proliferative arrest in RIS cells.
source: Oxidative stress is a key metabolic feature of RAS-induced senescence and ROS triggers DNA damage and proliferative arrest in RIS cells (Irani et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999; Ogrunc et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Irani et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999; Ogrunc et al., 2014).

claim: One major ROS-scavenging mechanism by the PI3K/AKT pathway is through sustained activation of NRF2.
source: One major ROS-scavenging mechanism by the PI3K/AKT pathway is through sustained activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) (Mitsuishi et al., 2012; Rada et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Mitsuishi et al., 2012; Rada et al., 2011).

claim: CBS deficiency in human gastric cancer cells is associated with hyper-methylation at the CBS promoter region.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated CBS deficiency in human gastric cancer cells with hyper-methylation at the CBS promoter region, implicating loss of CBS through epigenetic regulation in gastric cancer (Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Zhao et al., 2012).

claim: Cysteine starvation induces necrosis and ferroptosis in cancer cells.
source: Cysteine starvation has been reported to induce necrosis and ferroptosis in cancer cells (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Chen et al., 2017).

claim: Upregulation of xCT facilitates RAS-mediated transformation.
source: The expression level of xCT was also slightly upregulated during RIS, albeit to a lesser extent than during AIS, in line with the finding that upregulation of xCT facilitates RAS-mediated transformation (Lim et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Lim et al., 2019).

claim: A non-canonical mitochondrial targeting signal resides within C-terminal CBSD2 motif.
source: A non-canonical mitochondrial targeting signal has been reported to reside within C-terminal CBSD2 motif (Teng et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Teng et al., 2013).

claim: AKT overexpression promotes CBS translocation to mitochondria and subsequently increases energy metabolism to sustain the senescence state.
source: Collectively, our results strongly support the concept that AKT overexpression promotes CBS translocation to mitochondria and subsequently increases energy metabolism to sustain the senescence state.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental findings showing increased mitochondrial CBS, OCR, and ATP production in AIS cells.

claim: Increased levels of GSH and H2S through the transsulfuration pathway during AIS maintenance enhance the antioxidant capacity of AIS cells, protecting senescent cells from ROS-induced cell death.
source: Thus, we propose that increased levels of GSH and H2S through the transsulfuration pathway during AIS maintenance enhance the antioxidant capacity of AIS cells, protecting senescent cells from ROS-induced cell death (Figure 5J).
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing increased GSH and H2S in AIS cells and protective effects against oxidative stress.

claim: AKT-dependent increase of the antioxidant capacity is retained in CBS-deficient cells and contributes to escape of AIS cells from cell cycle arrest.
source: Importantly, this AKT-dependent increase of the antioxidant capacity is retained in CBS-deficient cells and thus contributes to escape of AIS cells from cell cycle arrest (Figure 4J).
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing maintained GSH and H2S levels in CBS-depleted AIS cells.

claim: Increased oxidative phosphorylation and ROS production sustain AIS status that require CBS.
source: Together, these results strongly support the concept that increased oxidative phosphorylation and ROS production sustain AIS status that require CBS.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing CBS depletion reduces OCR, ATP production, and ROS levels, leading to AIS escape.

claim: Loss of CBS can cooperate with oncogenic activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway to promote tumorigenesis.
source: Given that we showed CBS loss promotes escape from AIS, we hypothesized that loss of CBS could cooperate with oncogenic activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway to promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental findings showing CBS loss promotes AIS escape.

claim: CBS is a tumor suppressor in gastric cancers characterized by PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway alterations.
source: Furthermore, CBS mRNA level was significantly decreased in tumors (N=406) compared to adjacent normal tissues (N=211) in gastric cancer patients (Figure 6B), consistent with the hypothesis that CBS is a tumor suppressor in gastric cancers characterized by PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway alterations.
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis and experimental findings showing CBS loss cooperates with PI3K/AKT activation.

claim: Restoration of CBS expression could suppress gastric tumor formation independent of p53.
source: Induction of CBS was also associated with a marked decrease in Ki67 expression and inhibitory RB phosphorylation without altering p53 and p21 expression levels in the tumor tissues, suggesting that restoration of CBS expression could suppress gastric tumor formation independent of p53 (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: Inferred from Western blot and IHC data showing changes in Ki67 and RB but not p53 and p21 (Figure 7H, I).

claim: The tumor-suppressive effect of CBS in gastric cancer cells may be mediated through H2S.
source: Whether the tumor-suppressive effect of CBS in gastric cancer cells is mediated through H2S requires further investigation.
evidence: Speculative statement requiring further investigation.

claim: CBS provides a new metabolic vulnerability that can be harnessed to target PI3K/AKT/mTORC1-driven cancers.
source: Taken together, our study identifies CBS as a novel regulator of AIS maintenance and a potential tumor suppressor in gastric cancer pathogenesis, potentially providing a new metabolic vulnerability that can be harnessed to target PI3K/AKT/mTORC1-driven cancers.
evidence: Speculative statement based on experimental findings.
